subject: physics

items.correct: All objects do, whatever their temperature happens to be
items.misconception: Only objects hot enough to glow red, orange or white
items.why: The everyday examples students meet - a fire, a grill, a filament lamp - are all glowing, so emission gets tied to visible heat. Emission happens at every temperature. An ice cube emits infrared radiation too, just far less of it each second.
items.random_wrong: Only objects that are warmer than the air near them

items.q: Two identical iron blocks are held at 30 °C and at 80 °C in the same room. Which statement about the infrared radiation they emit is correct?
items.correct: The 80 °C block emits more radiation in a given time
items.misconception: Neither block emits until it is hotter than the room air
items.why: The temperature-difference rule that governs conduction and net energy transfer is carried over onto the act of emission itself. Every body emits according to its own temperature. The temperature difference decides the NET transfer, not whether emission happens.
items.random_wrong: Both emit equally, since the blocks are identical

items.q: What happens to radiation that is incident on a perfect black body?
items.correct: All of the radiation is absorbed by the body
items.misconception: Most is absorbed, but a small part is reflected
items.why: Real black surfaces do reflect slightly, and students generalise from the imperfect objects in front of them. 'Perfect' is the whole point of the model: absorption is total, with zero reflection and zero transmission.
items.random_wrong: It is all absorbed and stays trapped in the body

items.q: A perfect black body would be the best possible emitter of radiation. Why?
items.correct: A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter
items.misconception: It stores the radiation it absorbs and lets it out later
items.why: Absorption is pictured as trapping or storing, which makes emission sound like the opposite of absorption. Absorption and emission go together. The surface that absorbs best at a given wavelength also emits best at it.
items.random_wrong: Its surface is black, and black surfaces look hottest

items.q: An ice cube at −15 °C is put on a plate in a warm room. Which statement about the ice cube is correct?
items.correct: It emits radiation, but it absorbs more than it emits
items.misconception: It absorbs radiation but is much too cold to emit
items.why: Cold is treated as an absence of energy, so a cold object is imagined to have nothing to give out. There is no threshold temperature for emission. A colder body emits less each second, but it never stops emitting.
items.random_wrong: It only absorbs, because the room around it is warm

items.q: A lamp filament is heated from dull red to bright white. How does the radiation it emits change?
items.correct: The intensity rises and the peak moves to shorter waves
items.misconception: Only the intensity rises; the wavelength range is unchanged
items.why: Emitter quality really does depend on surface and material, so students extend that to mean temperature makes no difference. Material fixes how good an emitter a surface is; temperature fixes how much it emits and at which wavelengths.
items.random_wrong: Only the peak shifts; the intensity stays the same

items.q: Two stars are the same size. Star A looks blue-white and star B looks red. What can be concluded?
items.correct: Star A is hotter, and its peak wavelength is shorter
items.misconception: Star B is hotter, since red light carries more energy
items.why: Hotter is associated with 'more' of everything, and students read 'more' as a bigger wavelength number. Hotter bodies emit more of their radiation at short wavelengths - a filament goes from dull red to blue-white as it heats.
items.random_wrong: Star A is cooler, as blue light has a shorter wavelength

items.q: (HT only) A metal plate inside a hot oven has reached a constant temperature. What does this tell you about the radiation?
items.correct: It absorbs radiation as fast as it emits it
items.misconception: It has stopped absorbing and emitting any radiation
items.why: 'Nothing is changing' is read as 'nothing is happening', so a dynamic balance is mistaken for no activity at all. Both processes continue at full rate. They are equal, so there is no net transfer and the temperature holds steady.
items.random_wrong: It still absorbs radiation but no longer emits any

items.q: (HT only) The temperature of a body is rising. Which statement must be true?
items.correct: It is absorbing radiation faster than it emits radiation
items.misconception: It absorbs and emits radiation at the same rate
items.why: Absorption alone is linked to warming, and the emission going on at the same time is left out of the account. It is the balance that matters. A body absorbing radiation can still cool if it emits even faster than it absorbs.
items.random_wrong: It is absorbing radiation and emitting none at all

items.q: (HT only) Which factors does the temperature of the Earth depend on?
items.correct: The rates of absorption and emission, and reflection to space
items.misconception: Only how close the Earth sits to the Sun in space
items.why: Distance is the one factor that is easy to picture, and it does control how much radiation arrives. Arriving radiation is only the start. What is reflected away, what is absorbed and what is emitted all matter.
items.random_wrong: Only the distance of the Earth from the Sun and its orbit

items.q: (HT only) The ground cools quickly on a clear night, but much less on a cloudy night. Why?
items.correct: Cloud radiates energy back down, so the net loss is smaller
items.misconception: Cloud acts as an insulating layer, stopping conduction of heat
items.why: 'Blanket' is used loosely in everyday talk about cloud cover, and insulation is a far more familiar idea than radiation. The mechanism is radiative: the ground still emits, but it also absorbs radiation coming back down from the cloud.
items.random_wrong: Cloud completely stops the ground emitting radiation upwards

items.q: (HT only) An energy-balance diagram shows short-wavelength radiation arriving from the Sun and long-wavelength radiation leaving the Earth's surface. Why is the outgoing radiation longer in wavelength?
items.correct: The surface of the Earth is far cooler than the Sun
items.misconception: The radiation loses energy as it travels up through the air
items.why: Waves are imagined to tire out over distance, so a change of wavelength gets explained by the journey. Wavelength is set by the temperature of the emitter. The cool surface emits infrared; the very hot Sun emits much shorter waves.
items.random_wrong: The atmosphere stretches the waves as they pass through

items.q: Do shiny silver surfaces emit radiation?
items.correct: Yes, but they are poor emitters compared with dull black surfaces.
items.misconception: Only dull black surfaces emit radiation; shiny surfaces emit none at all.
items.why: Practicals comparing the faces of a Leslie cube show a large difference, which students read as 'emits' versus 'does not emit'. All surfaces emit. Colour and finish change how good an emitter a surface is, not whether it emits at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the intensity at each wavelength as a body is heated?
items.correct: The intensity rises at every wavelength, and the peak shifts as well.
items.misconception: Heating only shifts the peak; the total radiation emitted stays the same.
items.why: Attention fixes on the peak because it is the most obvious feature of the curve, so the rise in height is missed. Both change together: the whole curve rises and its peak moves to shorter wavelengths.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to radiation reflected by clouds and ice?
items.correct: It returns to space without ever warming the Earth's surface.
items.misconception: Reflected radiation is absorbed first, so it still warms the Earth a little.
items.why: Reflection and absorption both happen 'at the surface', so students blur the two together into one process. Reflected radiation is turned back before any energy is transferred, which is why bright surfaces keep the Earth cooler.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a body absorb and emit radiation at the same moment?
items.correct: Yes. Absorption and emission go on together, all the time.
items.misconception: A body does one or the other: while it is absorbing radiation it is not emitting any.
items.why: The two words describe opposite directions of transfer, so they get treated as alternatives that cannot both be happening. They run simultaneously and independently. It is the difference between the two rates that changes the temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.3 Black body radiation (physics only)
